newsitem.title: UK: Iraq snubs British requests for oil sale contracts.
newsitem.headline: Iraq snubs British requests for oil sale contracts.

text.p: Richard Mably

Iraq on Thursday snubbed British oil companies as Baghdad made clear it would favour "friendly" nations in awarding crude export contracts under the second phase of a United Nations oil-for-aid exchange.
Anglo-Dutch Shell and British Petroleum both said Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) had decided against renewing the companies' contracts.
Japanese traders said they too had received signals indicating they might not get Baghdad's blessing for fresh contracts.
"We had asked to renew our existing contract. We have been unofficially advised by SOMO that we would not receive an allocation," said a spokesman for BP.
"Our contract has not been renewed and we are awaiting the outcome of enquiries to clarify the matter," said a Shell spokesman.
Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Rasheed said in Baghdad on Wednesday that companies from countries deemed friendly to Iraq would get preferential treatment for oil sale contracts.
Rasheed said he expected to revive exports in mid-August after the final piece of a jigsaw for sales to restart fell into place at the United Nations on Tuesday.
The arrangement, designed to help Iraqi civilians, is an exception to sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Iraq has lobbied hard at the U.N. for a complete lifting of sanctions but has met implacable opposition from the United States and Britain.
Baghdad also blames those two countries and Japan for delaying aid contracts under the UN exchange.
Japanese oil refiners on Thursday said they were concerned that Iraq would decide not to renew contracts because of political differences with Tokyo.
"We have been notified by our head office that Baghdad has decided not to allocate to Japan in August," said a Singapore trader with a Japanese refiner that was also pursuing Iraqi barrels.
Japanese companies as a whole are hoping to secure at least 40,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi exports.
Both Mitsubishi Corp, which is representing four Japan refiners, and Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd have sent negotiators to Baghdad for contract talks.
By contrast, French oil companies Elf and Total said they were confident of renewing their contracts.
"For us it is business as usual with SOMO. We are confident of signing a new deal of the same size as our current deal," said a Total spokesman.
U.S. oil companies Mobil, Chevron and Texaco, which all bought Iraqi crude in the first phase of the deal, declined any immediate contract on whether they expected to secure new purchases.
Traders said they expected Russian oil companies to increase liftings.
Analysts said Baghdad might be playing political favourites but that oil sales would proceed in any case.
"There is obviously a strong political bias but the oil will still hit the market and may push prices lower," said John Toalster at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull Securities.
